# Results — Study 105 (Coppock-Curve) on real monthly tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One recipe — the Coppock Curve
(WMA(10) of ROC(14)+ROC(11) on monthly closes), buy when it turns up from below zero
(deduped: first uptick per cluster only) — tested on ^GSPC monthly since 1950 and on SPY
since 1993. Forward 6- and 12-month log returns are measured and compared against a
**random-timing control** (same signal count, randomly selected months) and the
**buy-and-hold baseline** (all months). As-of **2026-06-13**; match the per-tape fingerprint
to confirm you hold the same tape.*

## The honest test — 12-month forward return, ^GSPC, cost = 5 bps round-trip

| Arm | n | hit-rate | mean log ret | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Coppock buy** | 19 | **89.5%** | **+16.1%** | **+5.74** |
| Random timing | 19 | 68.4% | +1.6% | +0.28 |
| Buy-and-hold (all months) | 906 | 74.5% | +7.8% | — |

- **Coppock gross mean = +16.1% per signal** vs buy-and-hold's +7.8%. Delta = **+8.3 ppt**.
- Delta vs random-timing control = **+14.5 ppt** — large in absolute terms.
- HAC *t* = **+5.74** on the Coppock mean alone — *but* with only **n = 19 signals**,
  the Newey-West estimator has very few degrees of freedom; the practical inference bar
  is higher than the headline t-stat suggests. The classical t-test gives *t* = +5.06
  (vs 0) and *t* = +2.60 (vs buy-and-hold mean), *p* = 0.018.

## The honest test — 6-month forward return, ^GSPC

| Arm | n | hit-rate | mean log ret | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Coppock buy** | 19 | **84.2%** | **+7.9%** | **+4.43** |
| Random timing | 19 | 63.2% | +3.6% | +1.68 |
| Buy-and-hold | 912 | 70.3% | +3.9% | — |

- The 6-month picture is weaker: Coppock (7.9%) slightly beats BaH (3.9%) but the
  delta vs random (4.3 ppt) is smaller. Classical *t* vs BaH mean = +1.71 (*p* = 0.104).

## Critical caveats — why the verdict is WEAK, not REAL

1. **Tiny n.** 19 signals over 76 years. Any single signal (e.g., the 2001 signal, −26.6%)
   moves the mean substantially. A t-stat above 2 at n=19 is formally significant but
   the confidence interval spans several percentage points in each direction.
2. **Bear-market beta.** Coppock fires disproportionately after drawdowns (average 24m
   drawdown at signal: −14.3% vs −5.8% for all months). Much of the outperformance is
   simply timing beta at a cheap point in the cycle — a long-only investor already has
   this by staying invested through the recovery.
3. **Lagging by construction.** The warm-up is 23 months. By the time Coppock fires, the
   market has typically already recovered substantially from its trough. The 2009 signal
   (May 2009) came 2 months *after* the March 2009 bottom; the 1975 signal came 12 months
   after the December 1974 trough.
4. **No out-of-sample test.** Coppock published in 1962 on pre-1962 US data. The post-1962
   record (12 signals) continues to look good, but 12 is not enough for robust inference.
5. **Survivorship / market selection.** Tested only on the US equity index — arguably the
   single most bull-biased developed-market long-run series. Results on international markets
   are more mixed (literature is less clear).

## SPY (1993–2026, 5 signals)

With only 5 signals on SPY (n too small for t-stats), the point estimate is directionally
consistent (12m Coppock mean +27% vs BaH +12%) but effectively anecdotal at n=5.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The HAC t-stat is formally large (+5.74 at 12m), but n=19 makes the
  inference fragile. The signal *appears* real on the full 1950–2026 series; however, the
  bear-market beta confound, the small n, and the lagging nature make this a WEAK rather
  than a REAL verdict. Literature support (Coppock 1962) exists but the original derivation
  was spiritual, not statistical.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The signal itself might have economic timing merit (buying near
  bear-market recovery), but: (a) only ~1 signal every 4 years — not a strategy in the
  usual sense; (b) the Dec 2001 failure shows single signals can lose 26%; (c) the "edge"
  is essentially beta timing on a long-only index, not an alpha. An investor already holding
  the market has this without trading.
- **Beats buy-and-hold? — MIXED.** On the raw 12-month mean, Coppock (+16.1%) beats BaH
  (+7.8%) significantly in the small sample. But this is largely beta concentration at
  depressed entry points, not return alpha over a passive 12-month hold strategy — the BaH
  investor who did not sell already held through the same recovery.
